analysis.title: "Nothing Left To Drain": Goldman Finds Near-Record $22 Oil Risk Premium As Global Stocks Hit Rock Bottom
key_insights: Goldman's Oil Analyst note rebuilds its Brent model to include non-OECD visible stocks and finds a $22/bbl risk premium in September 2026, the second highest monthly reading on record after April 2026.
Using OECD commercial stocks alone, Goldman's model would imply a higher risk premium of $29/bbl, but that approach misses physical tightness outside the OECD.

Brent 1M/36M timespread has risen $30/bbl year-to-date while OECD commercial stocks have barely changed, so the old inventory relationship broke. In a sample back to 1998, OECD stocks explained over 60% of timespread variation.
Goldman estimates a 100mb (3.5%) decline in OECD commercial stocks raises Brent fair value by nearly $8/bbl, versus just over $2/bbl for a 100mb (3%) decline in other visible global landed stocks.

A 1mb/d supply loss lasting six months adds about $6.5/bbl to Brent fair value. The article's own napkin math: a $22 premium equals roughly 3.4mb/d of additional six-month supply loss that has not happened.

Vitol CEO Russell Hardy said there are no more inventories to drain in the West and that 10-14mb/d must leave the Gulf by ship to keep balance through winter. He also cited a $200/bbl scenario if the Hormuz shuttle stops working.

Hardy estimates about 12mn b/d of crude and 2mn b/d of refined fuels are leaving the Gulf since the US Navy cleared a route for Hormuz shuttle tankers. He describes the crisis as moving from a crude crisis to a product crisis to a shipping crisis.
Tanker charter rates are described as 'pretty parabolic'. An executive told the FT North Sea cargoes sold for $145/bbl last week and European refining margins turned negative.

John Kemp, using the EIA October STEO, shows global crude and product stocks at a critically low level. The article's sum of his monthly bars is roughly 660mb drawn in seven months since March, with close to 60% from non-OECD tanks. Every month since March except July was a draw.
Goldman's visible-stocks counter showed a cumulative 509mb draw since March 1 as of August.

JPMorgan's Natasha Kaneva reads the headline 100mb emergency release as largely the completion of the earlier IEA release (400mb announced earlier this year), not new barrels, with a stronger focus on diesel.
US SPR fell another 784K barrels to 283MM, just 13MM above the lowest level since inception in 1982.

Dated Brent trades more than $20 above the front-month future, the widest since the March panic. Spot North Sea Forties was quoted above $140/bbl, the highest since the war began. Diesel crack spreads went back over $100.

Goldman names three drivers of the premium: supply-disruption fears (correlation 0.5 with Brent call skew and a news-based geopolitical risk index), speculative positioning (correlation 0.6 since 2023), and macro portfolio hedging as oil supply shocks raise inflation and Treasury yields.
With the 10Y yield above 5.3%, the Brent to 10Y correlation is near the top of its 25-year range while the oil-stocks correlation has collapsed, so oil is acting as a hedge for bonds and stocks.
The peak monthly risk premium after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine did not exceed $16/bbl, per Goldman.

Goldman's base case has the premium gradually returning to its historical average of zero, but it warns the premium may stay elevated until a clear diplomatic resolution. It sees upside risk to its price forecast if geopolitics keep the premium elevated longer.

Goldman's 3-year-ahead Brent fair value is $76, including a $9 security premium added at the start of the war. Its forecast was raised last month, with Brent possibly reaching $120 if Hormuz disruptions last into 2027.

Recent shocks: tanker attacked off Qatar, IRGC strike on an LPG tanker in Hormuz, Saudi media reports of Houthis mining Bab al-Mandab, Hurricane Isaias shutting in 63% of US Gulf oil output, Ukrainian drones reportedly hitting a major Russian fuel export hub, and Trump saying he won't attack Iran before the midterms.

sector_views.rationale: Goldman sees upside risk to its Brent forecast if the risk premium stays elevated, and the article argues inventories are depleted so a small disruption has outsized price consequences.

tension_points.bull_case: Inventories are near record lows (about 660mb drawn since March), the SPR is 13MM above its record low, the 100mb release is not new, and the premium is driven by fear, positioning and hedge demand, so Brent can stay elevated or rise toward Goldman's $120 scenario and Vitol's $200 scenario.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman's base case has the premium gradually returning to zero as Middle East supply keeps beating expectations on adaptability. Hormuz flows have recovered, Russian diesel may arrive, and a diplomatic deal could remove the premium.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A clear diplomatic resolution, or Hormuz flows continuing without new disruption while Russian diesel arrives, would undercut the elevated-premium view.
